data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more probable or true, but as a critical rational choice to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe tests so far, accepting the cost that this preference offers no guarantee of future success and remains perpetually open to falsification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a probabilistic guarantee of future success to act, Popper's framework cannot provide it without smuggling in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) is invoked as the metric for preference, the Tich\u00fd-Miller theorem undermines its formal coherence within Popper's system.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is interpreted as a causal explanation for why the theory will continue to work (evolutionary analogy), it conflates descriptive survival with normative justification.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Rational Choice via Severe Testing: The mechanism distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which never gains probability) and the methodological rule for action (prefer the theory that has survived the most rigorous attempts at refutation). This avoids induction by treating corroboration as a report on past performance under stress, not a predictor of future frequency. The 'preference' is a decision to bet on the currently least-refuted option, acknowledging that the next test could overturn it.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
